phonemes.desc: Long diphthong αι [ai̯] carrying the acute pitch accent; the alpha is open and the iota forms an off-glide.
Long alpha [aː] followed by voiceless sibilant [s], the nominal ending of the hero's name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-yahs' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the final syllable is open and sustained.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Αἴας (Aias), the bulwark of the Achaeans in the Iliad

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Ajax, the Roman rendering adopted into English and many modern languages

kin.label: Pre-Greek
kin.form: Beekes classes Αἴας as Pre-Greek; the name resists Indo-European analysis like many -ās hero names

pronunciation.note: The Greek Αἴας contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (long alpha in the diphthong and final syllable), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Ajax is a secondary spelling, not the original Greek.

domains.title: The Bulwark of the Achaeans
domains.subtitle: Warrior, Defender, and Unyielding Will
domains.lead: Aias is the great defensive warrior of the Greek army at Troy. In the Iliad he is second only to Achilles in strength and courage, a tower of bronze and stubbornness who saves the Greek ships from fire, duels Hector to a standstill, and carries the dead Achilles from the field. Where Achilles is speed and wrath, Aias is mass, endurance, and absolute loyalty. His name became a byword for the soldier who holds the line when everything else breaks.

cards.name: The Shield Wall
cards.desc: Aias fights with a towering seven-fold oxhide shield that protects whole companies, not merely himself.

cards.name: Duel with Hector
cards.desc: He meets Hector in single combat and fights him to a draw, proving that defence can match offence.

cards.name: Rescue of Achilles
cards.desc: After Achilles falls, Aias stands over the body and bears Achilles' corpse from the battlefield.

cards.name: Tragic Pride
cards.desc: Denied Achilles' armour, he falls into a madness of shame and takes his own life on the seashore.

symbols.name: Seven-fold oxhide shield
symbols.meaning: The massive tower-shield that makes Aias a living fortress and protects the whole Greek line.

symbols.name: Sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon with which he slays sheep in his madness and then himself in the tragedy of Sophocles.

symbols.name: The ships
symbols.meaning: The beached Greek fleet that Aias defends when the Trojans press it with fire.

symbols.name: The seashore
symbols.meaning: The place of his suicide and burial, where the waves meet the land of Troy.

mythology.lead: The myths of Aias are told in the Iliad, the lost Epic Cycle, and above all in Sophocles' tragedy Aias. They turn on a single quality: the absolute, unbending commitment of the warrior. That quality makes him the Greeks' greatest defender and, when it is slighted, their most terrible casualty.

myths.title: The Defence of the Ships
myths.text: When the Trojans broke the Greek wall and reached the beached ships, fire was set to Protesilaus' vessel, and the whole Achaean cause hung on a deck. There Homer stations Aias: striding from prow to stern behind his seven-fold oxhide shield, a pike twenty-two cubits long, holding the Trojans off while men rallied behind him (Iliad 15.674–746). Earlier, as Hector cut through the ranks, the poet had compared him to a donkey that boys cannot drive from a cornfield — stubborn, scorned, immovable (Iliad 11.558–562). When even Aias must yield at last, he does so grudgingly, calling the retreat a disaster (Iliad 16.101–111). The Defence of the Ships is the Iliad's hymn to the unglamorous virtue: endurance. Achilles wins the poem's glory; Aias saves its army. Homer seems to know that civilizations stand less on brilliance than on the man who refuses, step by bloody step, to move.

myths.title: Duel with Hector
myths.text: Hector challenges the Greeks to single combat, and the lots fall to Telamonian Aias — the biggest man among them, Homer says, save Achilles (Iliad 7.206–312). The duel fills a book: spear-casts stopped on shield and breastplate, a stone that spins Hector like a top, nightfall parting them at last. Neither yields; each wins honor, and they exchange gifts — Hector's sword and scabbard for Aias's scarlet belt. Homer comments in one terrible line: 'bad gifts' — for Aias will one day fall on Hector's sword, and Hector's corpse will be dragged behind Achilles' chariot by the very belt Aias gave. The duel is the Iliad's picture of war's fairness: two men of equal worth meet, measure each other, and part with respect — while the narrator, who knows how both die, lets us feel the courtesy and the doom in a single gesture. Equality is real; so is what comes after.

myths.title: The Rescue of Achilles' Body
myths.text: Achilles fell at the Scaean gates, struck down by Paris with Apollo's help. The Greeks' greatest corpse became the day's greatest battle. Aias and Odysseus fought through to the body — Odysseus holding the Trojans at bay while Aias heaved the dead hero onto his shoulders and carried him from the field, Achilles' armor in his other arm (Aethiopis, in Proclus' summary; Quintus of Smyrna, Posthomerica 3). It was the last and largest of Aias's labors for the army that would soon betray him: the strong man carrying what the army could not afford to lose, doing the work glory forgot to record. Homer remembers the end — Achilles' ashes mingled with Patroclus' in a golden urn for 'the best of the Achaeans' (Odyssey 24.43–84) — but does not say who bore him there. The silence is the point: Aias's loyalty needed no witness, and asked for none.

myths.title: The Madness and Suicide
myths.text: The armor of Achilles was the prize of the war, and the Greeks awarded it — by the army's shouting, Sophocles says — to Odysseus. Aias, broken by the judgment, was driven mad by Athena: by night he fell upon the flocks, butchering sheep he took for the sons of Atreus. Sanity returned to the sight of his own disgrace (Ajax 1–133, 284–330). 'A glorious death or a life of shame,' he cried, and chose: planting Hector's gifted sword upright in the sand of the seashore, he fell upon it — the only hero of the Trojan war to die by his own hand, and the first great suicide in Western literature. Sophocles lets the army debate his burial: Menelaus would leave him to the dogs; Odysseus, of all people, argues for honor — 'I hated him while it was honorable to hate' (Ajax 1355–1361). The play that preserves Aias is also the earliest portrait of combat trauma: the wound not in the body but in the code, honor turned inward until it kills. Modern armies still stage it for their soldiers, and it still explains what it was written to explain.

lore.syncretism: Aias was honoured as a hero at Salamis, his father's island, and at Athens, where the festival Aianteia included games in his honour. The Athenians claimed him as their own through his father Telamon's exile there. Roman writers such as Ovid retold his story, and the name Ajax passed into modern culture as a byword for physical might and tragic pride. In the twentieth century it became a brand name for cleaning products and football clubs, a long descent from the Homeric bulwark.
lore.culturalLegacy: Aias stands at the centre of Western reflection on military honour and mental injury. Sophocles' tragedy is now read as one of the earliest literary explorations of combat trauma and the violence that shame can turn inward. The American Department of Defense has sponsored performances of the play for veterans. The Ajax football club of Amsterdam takes its name and emblem from the hero, and 'Ajax' has been used for military vehicles, ships, and spacecraft. His story reminds us that the strongest defender may be the most vulnerable when honour is denied.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aias teaches that strength without flexibility can become its own enemy. His refusal to bend before the Greek commanders is the same refusal that let him hold the ships against Hector; turned inward, it becomes the sword with which he destroys himself. The modern reader cannot easily judge him. His suicide is at once a failure of proportion and a terrible assertion of dignity.

To remember Aias is to remember the cost of asking human beings to be shields. The wall that protects others must itself bear every blow. When the wall is slighted, the whole structure of honour trembles.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Αἴας. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent; the final alpha is long. The Latin form Ajax and English Ajax are secondary spellings that mask the original Greek vowel quantities. The PuniCodex restoration Aias recovers the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because both pitch accent and vowel length are preserved.
